problems.description: Replaced the seed's modular Blueprint-based structure with a flat, single-file app.py (all routes as free functions). This monolith will strain the story's later sessions (JWT auth, Celery worker, repository refactor) which need the modular seams the seed provided.

AST diff shows +0 files, yet convention violations surface in untouched seed modules (repositories.py, tasks.py, celery_config.py, test_app.py). Rewriting only app.py while leaving those seed files behind orphans stale/contradictory modules, yielding a mixed architecture of flat new code plus dead seed code.
Cognitive complexity +35 despite -220 lines — the new handlers are more convoluted per line than the code they replaced; this is debt that Session 2-5 must untangle.
Convention score 0.67 with 9 violations (classes should use PascalCase, module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE, functions should use snake_case) across app.py and related modules.
+7 functions added with +0 classes; no evidence the new endpoints (GET /tasks/{id}, PUT /tasks/{id}) and 404/400 paths are covered — the spec requires all endpoints to pass pytest.

strengths: Delivers the correct domain for story Session 1: task CRUD, SQLite persistence, status default 'pending', ordering by created_at desc.
Smells -4 and +0 new bugs: removed the insecure hardcoded-salt sha256 hashing from the seed.
Uses timezone-aware datetime (datetime.now(timezone.utc)) instead of naive datetime.utcnow().
Validates title input (rejects non-string/blank with 400) and returns structured JSON errors.
Zero duplications (0.0%) and a leaner surface (-220 lines).
commit_reviews.summary: Correct greenfield domain but an architectural regression: it flattens the seed's modular Blueprint layout into a convoluted single-file monolith (complexity +35) while leaving stale seed modules behind — the convention score of 0.67 (9 violations, concentrated in untouched files) is worse than my qualitative read of the visible app.py diff, which is otherwise clean.

problems.description: Hand-rolled JWT (manual HS256 via hmac) instead of a vetted library like PyJWT; reinventing token cryptography invites subtle vulnerabilities and needless maintenance burden.
JWT_SECRET falls back to secrets.token_hex(32) per process when SECRET_KEY is unset, so tokens become invalid on restart and cannot be shared across workers.
Schema migration (ALTER TABLE, legacy-user backfill) is embedded in init_db, coupling migration logic to app startup with no versioning as the schema grows.
Measured convention score 0.67 with 9 violations across touched files (PascalCase classes, UPPER_CASE constants, snake_case functions); commit neither fixes nor consistently follows the naming rules.
Bearer token returned on login but register returns only user info; client must make a second call — acceptable but worth noting in API design.

strengths: Uses werkzeug's generate/check_password_hash rather than hand-rolled password hashing
Constant-time signature comparison via hmac.compare_digest
Token verification validates the signature before trusting claims, and rejects non-int 'sub' and expired tokens
Follows existing Flask idioms: decorator-based auth, g for current_user, get_db context manager, idempotent init_db
Includes tests (test_app.py in diff) for the new auth paths
commit_reviews.summary: Commit adds a well-structured JWT auth + user model that fits the existing single-file Flask patterns and ships with tests, but hand-rolls token crypto and a random per-process secret, matching the measured 0.67 convention score and adding moderate technical debt.

problems.description: Notification enqueueing happens inline in the request handler (update_task), coupling the write path to the broker; mitigated by the try/except guard but a post-commit hook or event would be cleaner at scale.
The `celery = celery_app` alias in celery_config.py is redundant documentation-only sugar; harmless but adds a second public name to maintain.
Using `g.current_user["username"]` as the contact address couples the notification payload to the auth model; acknowledged by a comment but a fragile assumption if auth changes.
Analyzer flags module-level `celery_app` and `logger` as needing UPPER_CASE, but this matches the existing lowercase `app = Flask(...)` instance pattern, so it is not a genuine deviation.

strengths: Correct transition-to-completed detection computed before the write, so idempotent updates do not double-notify
Graceful degradation: broker/Redis failure cannot fail the task update endpoint, and the failure is logged
Celery task has an explicit name and is routed to a dedicated 'notifications' queue
Tests cover both the enqueue path and the no-enqueue-on-non-transition path
Small, focused diff that keeps notification logic in a separate module rather than bloating app.py
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-tested integration that adds async completion notifications with correct transition semantics and graceful broker failure handling; the measured convention score of 0.67 is misleading because 8 of the 9 flagged violations are analyzer false positives (repositories.py is not even in this diff, no classes or functions were added where claimed), so my qualitative convention judgment of ~0.85 deliberately departs from the mechanical score.

problems.description: New file repositories.py introduces a module-level constant not in UPPER_CASE (per measurement), the only convention violation attributable to this commit; the rest are pre-existing in untouched files (celery_config.py, tasks.py, test_app.py, app.py classes).
SonarQube cognitive complexity rose +55 despite the net -3 smells reduction, indicating the new BaseRepository/helper abstraction adds measurable complexity worth simplifying.

Repositories open a fresh sqlite3 connection per method call, bypassing Flask's request-scoped get_db()/g connection lifecycle used elsewhere, so no request-scoped transaction span and duplicated connection handling.

strengths: Centralizes schema creation and legacy migration into initialize_database, removing the inline DDL/PRAGMA logic from app.py
Extracts ~99 lines of inline SQL from route handlers into typed repository classes (TaskRepository, UserRepository)
Replaces raw sqlite3.IntegrityError handling with a domain exception DuplicateUserError for cleaner control flow
SonarQube confirms net improvement: -3 smells, 0 bugs, 0.0% duplication
commit_reviews.summary: A solid repository-pattern refactor that centralizes schema and data access and cuts smells by 3, held back only by minor nits — a non-UPPER_CASE constant in repositories.py, a +55 cognitive complexity bump, and per-call connections that bypass the existing request-scoped get_db()/g pattern.

problems.description: The @app.before_request hook swaps limiter.storage to MemoryStorage based on app.testing, mutating global state per request (order/fixture dependent, side-effectful), while the test fixture separately sets api.limiter._storage — two divergent mechanisms doing the same job. Storage should be configured once at Limiter construction.

Cursor pagination in page_for_owner filters on 'id < cursor' but orders by 'created_at DESC, id DESC'; the cursor encodes only id, so ties or non-monotonic created_at can skip or duplicate rows across pages. Keyset pagination should use the full ordering key (created_at, id).
_count runs a full COUNT(*) scan on every page and rows are materialized to limit+1 before slicing; acceptable at this scale but unbounded as the table grows.
rate_limit_key calls verify_token() on every request just to build a limiter key, incurring a DB/token lookup per request even for malformed or absent tokens.
Default page limit (20) is duplicated across the route default and the page_for_owner signature; a shared constant would prevent drift.
RATE_LIMIT_STORAGE_URI defaults to redis://localhost:6379, adding a production Redis dependency to an otherwise SQLite-centered codebase; acceptable since env-driven, but worth noting in docs.

strengths: Rate limiting keyed by authenticated subject rather than IP alone is a strong security design
MemoryStorage test path avoids requiring an external Redis process in CI
Cursor-based pagination avoids offset-scan degradation and rejects invalid params with clear 400s
page_for_owner and _count slot cleanly into the existing BaseRepository/TaskRepository helper conventions
Thorough tests: pagination flow, invalid-parameter matrix, 429 + Retry-After, and auth-endpoint limiting
commit_reviews.summary: A solid feature commit (rate limiting + cursor pagination) that respects repository and route conventions, but the test-only limiter storage swap and id-only cursor ordering add minor technical debt. Convention score (0.67) is dragged down mostly by pre-existing violations in untouched files (celery_config.py, tasks.py); the new code itself is stylistically consistent.

compounding_issues: Session 1 discarded the seed's modular Blueprint/JWT/auth structure and rebuilt a single-file app; session 2 then had to reimplement auth and JWT from scratch instead of inheriting it
app.py remained a ~260-line monolith even after the session 4 repository refactor — JWT encoding/decoding, rate limiting, and all route handlers stayed in app.py
Session 2 hand-rolled a custom HMAC-HS256 JWT implementation (base64/urllib) rather than using a standard JWT library, keeping security-sensitive crypto in application code
Binary artifacts leaked into git history starting session 2 and accumulated: __pycache__/*.pyc files committed in session 2, plus a tasks.db and more .pyc files committed in session 4
requirements.txt was only added in the final session despite Flask being a dependency since session 1, so earlier sessions had no pinned dependency manifest
key_decisions: Choosing a single-file Flask app for the session 1 greenfield instead of preserving the seed's Blueprint-based multi-file structure
Adding a SQLite migration path in session 2 (ALTER TABLE to add owner_id + legacy-user backfill) to preserve pre-auth data rather than resetting the schema
Adopting Celery + Redis as the async notification worker in session 3, triggered from PUT /tasks/{id} with an exception guard so broker failure never breaks the API response
Extracting the Repository pattern in session 4 (BaseRepository ABC + TaskRepository/UserRepository) — the largest structural change, which kept all raw SQL out of route handlers
Implementing Flask-Limiter with Redis storage plus a MemoryStorage swap for tests, and cursor-based pagination returning {data, next_cursor, total} in session 5
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across the five sessions. Test coverage grew from a smoke test in session 1 to 4 passing tests in session 2, 6 in session 3, and 13 passing in session 5 (verified against the final commit). Each session layered features coherently — CRUD, then auth, then async notifications, then a repository refactor, then rate limiting and pagination — with session 5 building directly on session 4's TaskRepository.page_for_owner and session 2's auth layer. The only quality dip was transient: session 4's refactor initially broke 2 tests (2 failed, 4 passed) before recovering to 6 passing in the same session, and session 5 notably recovered from an early 6-test pass to a full 13-test pass. The main regression was hygiene, not functionality: build artifacts (compiled .pyc files and a runtime tasks.db) progressively accumulated in the committed tree.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, textbook 5-session progression (greenfield → auth → integration → refactor → cross-cutting) that compounded features successfully and landed at 13 passing tests, with the main shortcomings being early architectural disposal of the seed's auth machinery and accumulating binary-artifact hygiene debt.
